how-much-to-charge-to-install-carpet.htm.text:
← Carpet installation bid calculator

How much to charge to install carpet

Carpet installers get shopped on a published $2 a yard installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the stairs or the waste. A flat living-room stretch is a different job from a patterned glue-down with fourteen stairs, a tear-out, and a furniture move.

Open the free carpet installation bid calculator

Price the floor and the stairs, not the $2-a-yard dump

A carpet install is a floor, then the stairs, then how the goods go down. Stretch-in over pad is the cheap living-room special. Glue-down is adhesive on a slab. Double-stick is both. Carpet tile wastes less roll. Solid is no match. Patterned is match waste and extra seaming. Stairs are priced per step: each wrap is tread, riser, and extra seaming that floor yards do not see.

Stairs are not yards

Homeowners usually start from the living-room special, then ask whether “the stairs are a little more.” On the same floor they are not a little more. Thirteen stairs buy wraps, extra seaming, and a different crew hour. The calculator prices 0, 7, 13, and 21 stairs on the floor you already measured so you can quote the wraps instead of matching the flat-floor number on a stair house.

Stretch-in is not a glue-down

The cheap special is almost always a solid stretch-in on a flat room, no tear-out, no furniture, no haul. A patterned glue-down with fourteen stairs is a different crew hour. Matching a per-yard number on a stair-and-tear-out job is how a sold carpet becomes a loss when the wraps and the dump ticket eat the margin.

This is not carpet cleaning or an LVP install

Carpet cleaning is steam, rooms, and pet urine. Flooring install is LVP, hardwood, and tile as hard-surface waste and tear-out. Epoxy is grind and flake. Hardwood refinishing is sand and finish. A kitchen backsplash is a wall. A walk-in shower is wet-area tile. This prices a carpet installation: the floor yards, the stairs, the stretch-versus-glue scope, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the carpet installation bid calculator. It is not a flooring-spec determination, a moisture test, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install carpet?

Charge from floor yards, stairs, stretch-versus-glue, patterned waste, and extras — not a published $2-a-yard special. A flat living-room stretch is a different job from a patterned glue-down with fourteen stairs, a tear-out, and a furniture move.

Are stairs the same bid as floor yards?

No. Stairs are priced per step: each wrap is tread, riser, and extra seaming. Floor yards do not see that labor. Matching a living-room special on a 13-stair house is how a sold carpet becomes a loss when the wraps eat the margin.

Is stretch-in the same bid as glue-down?

No. Stretch-in over pad is the cheap living-room special. Glue-down is adhesive on a slab. Double-stick is both. Carpet tile wastes less roll. Matching a stretch-in number on a glue-down job is the losing bid.

Is this the same as carpet cleaning or LVP install?

No. Carpet cleaning is steam, rooms, and pet urine. Flooring install is LVP, hardwood, and tile as hard-surface waste and tear-out. This prices a carpet installation: the floor yards, the stairs, the stretch-versus-glue scope, and extras.

Wondering whether the published $2-a-yard special actually covers a job? It does not even cover the carpet.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise “$2 a yard installed”?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a 400 sq ft flat living room, stretch-in over pad, solid colour, no stairs. It really does price low. What the per-yard number cannot see is scope (stretch-in vs. glue-down vs. double-stick), pattern match, stairs, transitions, tear-out, a furniture move, and haul-away. Price your actual floor beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items you can show the homeowner instead of an argument about who is honest.

    What is the real price difference between stretch-in, glue-down, and double-stick?

    They are different labor and different material. Stretch-in over pad starts at 0.11 install hours per yard with a pad cost and no adhesive — the cheap-special assumption. Glue-down skips the pad but adds adhesive and runs slower at 0.18 hours per yard because it is bonded to the slab. Double-stick glues both pad and carpet and is the slowest of the three at 0.22 hours per yard. Carpet tile wastes the least roll. Changing scope here refills the starting hours and material so you can see the swing before you type a single rate.

    Why are stairs priced separately instead of folded into floor yards?

    Because stairs are not yards. Each stair adds its own installer hours, its own billed yardage (stair yards each), and its own wrap material cost, on top of whatever the flat floor takes. The “same floor, four stair counts” table prices the identical floor at 0, 7, 13, and 21 stairs from the suggested extra kit so you can see how much a stair house adds over the flat special before you accidentally quote a 13-stair job at the flat-floor number.

    Why does a patterned carpet cost more than solid for the same square footage?

    Waste and seam time both go up. Solid colour starts at 10% waste with no pattern-matching hours. Patterned carpet starts at 18% waste plus extra hours per yard to match the pattern across every seam, and berber/loop carpet starts at 14% waste with its own care-on-seams-and-stairs hours. The “same floor, four scopes” comparison uses whatever pattern you selected, so the material and labor swing shows up in the price, not just in the waste percentage field.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s address rather than sending anything to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your floor size, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — crew hours, carpet and pad, stairs, tear-out, transitions, and haul-away — the point below which the install stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering into “Price you’re considering” shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price, which is how the customer's number is quoted and how your P&L reads it: price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin). Overhead, separately, is a markup on the direct cost of the job and is applied before margin, never to itself or to the profit. Marking a $3,000 cost up by 20% gives $3,600 and a 16.7% margin. Targeting a 20% margin gives $3,750 — a gap that is easy to give away across a whole season of bids typed the wrong way.

should-i-charge-2-a-yard-to-install-carp.text:
← Carpet installation bid calculator

Should I charge $2 a yard to install carpet?

An owner sends a screenshot: “$2 a yard, installed carpet.” It reads like a real quote. Run it against this calculator's own suggested rates and it isn't close on any job — not even the flat, no-stairs living room it was written for. On the cheapest preset, $2/yd doesn't clear the price of the carpet itself, before a single crew hour gets counted.

Open the free carpet installation bid calculator

$2 a yard doesn't cover any of the four presets

Using the calculator's own default crew rates (a $38 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, $55 travel and equipment) on the four jobs it ships as starting presets, each priced from its own floor, stairs, scope, pattern, and extras:

JobNet yd²$2/yd specialWalk-away priceVerdict
Cheap special: 400 sq ft living room, stretch-in, solid, no stairs44.4$88.89$2,167.01Loses $2,078.12
Typical house: 900 sq ft, stretch-in, solid, 13 stairs, tear-out, furniture100.0$200.00$6,361.54Loses $6,161.54
Losing job: 400 sq ft + 14 stairs, patterned glue-down, tear-out, haul44.4$88.89$3,919.59Loses $3,830.70
Whole house: 1,600 sq ft, 21 stairs, patterned, tear-out, furniture, haul177.8$355.56$12,199.63Loses $11,844.07

Every row loses, and not narrowly. $2/yd was never a walk-away price for any of these jobs — the calculator's own suggested carpet invoice runs $22 per billed yard before pad, adhesive, tack strip, or a single crew hour is counted.

$2 a yard doesn't cover the carpet, let alone the labor

Take the cheap special apart. The carpet invoice for that 400 sq ft floor — the raw material, nothing else — is $1,075.56. The $2/yd flyer price for the same floor is $88.89. The material alone is over twelve times the flyer's entire number, and the flyer hasn't yet paid for pad ($266.67 more), tack strip, the crew's 7.3 hours, or a dollar of overhead and margin. A number that low was never priced to be paid in full — it is written to get the phone to ring, not to install a real floor.

Same 400 square feet, worse on a stair house

The cheap special and the losing job share the exact same 400 sq ft floor, so $2/yd prices identically at $88.89 for either one. The only thing that changes between them is scope: a flat living-room stretch-in in solid colour versus a patterned glue-down with 14 stairs, a tear-out, and a haul-away. That difference alone takes the shortfall from $2,078.12 to $3,830.70 — about 1.8 times worse for the identical square footage, before the flyer's baseline shortfall is even considered.

This is a scope question, not a size question

The trap is not “the floor got bigger.” It is “the floor stayed the same size and picked up stairs, a glue-down slab, and a tear-out, and the per-yard number I quoted from never had those in it.” An installer who matches the flyer number on square footage alone — without checking whether the job is actually stretch-in or glue-down, solid or patterned, flat or full of stairs — is the one who finds out the wraps and the dump ticket ate the whole margin.

How to use the comparison

Open the carpet installation bid calculator, load the matching starting job from the “Choose a starting job…” preset list, and put the owner's per-yard number (times your net floor yards) into “price you're considering.” The calculator scores it against the walk-away price for the scope you actually priced, not the scope the flyer was written for.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install carpet and this calculator vs. MeasureSquare. It is not a flooring-spec determination, a moisture test, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

Should I charge $2 a yard to install carpet?

No. On the cheapest preset — a 400 sq ft living room, stretch-in over pad, solid colour, no stairs — $2 a yard on 44.4 net yards is $88.89. The carpet invoice alone for that floor is $1,075.56, and the full walk-away price is $2,167.01. The flyer number does not clear the material cost, let alone the labor.

Why doesn't $2 a yard even cover the carpet itself?

Because $2/yd is below wholesale. This calculator's own suggested carpet invoice is $22 per billed yard before pad, adhesive, tack strip, stairs, or a single crew hour. A flyer price that low was never meant to be paid in full — it is a number written to get the phone to ring, not a price anyone installs a real floor for.

Does the gap get worse on a stair house at the same square footage?

Yes. Both the cheap special and the losing job are 400 sq ft, so $2/yd prices identically at $88.89 for either. Add 14 stairs, a patterned glue-down, a tear-out, and a haul-away to that same floor and the shortfall against the walk-away price grows from $2,078.12 to $3,830.70 — about 1.8 times worse for the identical square footage.

should-i-charge-extra-for-moving-furnitu.text:
← Carpet installation bid calculator

Should I charge extra for moving furniture on a carpet install?

It comes up on the walkthrough, not the estimate sheet: “Can you just move the couch and the dresser too? Shouldn’t take you long.” It doesn’t take long — the calculator’s suggested rate is a flat 1.6 crew-hours — but “doesn’t take long” is not the same as “free,” and the easy answer on-site (“sure, no charge”) is a real number, not a courtesy.

Open the free carpet installation bid calculator

It is a flat line item, not a percentage of the floor

Furniture move is priced in this calculator as its own fixed crew task — 1.6 hours, independent of floor yards, scope, or pattern. At the calculator’s default crew rates ($38/hr wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin), that is $113.62 added to the price. Turn it on across the three built-in job presets and the add-on does not move with the size of the floor:

PresetPrice, no furniturePrice, with furnitureAdd-on
Cheap special — 400 sq ft, no stairs$2,708.76$2,822.38$113.62
Typical house — 900 sq ft, 13 stairs$7,838.30$7,951.92$113.62
Whole house — 1,600 sq ft, 21 stairs$15,135.92$15,249.54$113.62

Same add-on on a one-room job and a whole house, because the crew task itself — clear the floor, stage the pieces, set them back — does not scale with square footage the way carpet yardage or stair count does. That is also why folding it into a per-yard rate is the wrong place to hide it: raise the per-yard price enough to cover it on a small room and you overcharge a big one; price it low enough for the big house and the small room gives it away.

What “I’ll just do it for free” actually costs

On the typical-house preset (900 sq ft, 13 stairs, tear-out and haul included), pricing with the furniture move in the scope gives a total cost of $6,361.54 against a price of $7,951.92 — a profit of $1,590.38. Quote the no-furniture price of $7,838.30 instead because it felt awkward to add a line item on the walkthrough, then still move the furniture on install day, and the real cost is still $6,361.54. Profit falls to $1,476.76 — a giveaway of exactly $113.62, the identical number the line item would have charged. The favor is not free; it is unbilled.

This is not stairs, tear-out, or haul-away

The other extras in this calculator scale with the job: stairs are priced per step, tear-out and haul-away are priced per billed yard, so a bigger floor or a longer stair run costs more of each. Furniture move does not — it is one flat task whether the crew clears a studio apartment or a five-bedroom house with a set of stairs in between. Pricing it as a fixed line item is what keeps a small job from subsidizing a big one and a big job from swallowing the cost of a small one.

How to use the comparison

Open the carpet installation bid calculator, pick a preset or type your own floor, and toggle “Move furniture off the floor” on and off to see the add-on on your own rates — your wage, burden, overhead, and margin may not match the defaults above, so the dollar figure will move even though the underlying hours stay flat. This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install carpet; it is not a scheduling estimate for how long the move itself will take, and it is not a guarantee that 1.6 hours covers a house full of oversized furniture — replace the hours with your own crew's time for a heavier job.

Common questions

Should I charge extra for moving furniture on a carpet install?

Yes, as its own line item. Moving furniture off the floor is a flat 1.6 crew-hour task in this calculator's suggested rates. At a $38 wage with 30% burden that is $113.62 added to the price after overhead and margin — the same $113.62 whether the floor is a 400 sq ft living room or a 1,600 sq ft whole house, because the task does not get bigger with the floor.

Does the furniture-move charge change with the size of the job?

No, and that is the point. On the calculator's cheap-special (400 sq ft), typical-house (900 sq ft, 13 stairs), and whole-house (1,600 sq ft, 21 stairs) presets, turning on furniture move adds exactly $113.62 to the price every time. It is priced as fixed crew-hours, not a percentage of floor yards, so folding it into a per-yard rate either overcharges a small room or undercharges a big one.

What happens if I just move it for free instead of listing it?

You eat the cost with nothing to show for it. On the typical-house preset, quoting the no-furniture price of $7,838.30 but still moving the furniture drops actual profit from the intended $1,590.38 to $1,476.76 — a $113.62 giveaway, the identical figure the line item would have charged. Verbal goodwill on the walkthrough is a real, calculable pay cut unless the price moves with it.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-yard.html.text:
← Carpet Installation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per yard

“$55 a yard installed” is not a price for a carpet job — it is a price for one specific scope, pattern, and stair count, quietly applied to every floor that calls in.

What a flat rate per yard is

A flat rate per yard is the fastest way to quote: multiply the floor's billed yardage by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — a flat living-room stretch-in over pad, solid carpet, no stairs, no tear-out — and then reused for every floor afterward, whether or not the next floor looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the floor square footage, stair count, scope (stretch-in, glue-down, double-stick, or carpet tile), pattern (solid, textured, patterned, or berber), transitions, tear-out, furniture move, and haul-away, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the floor, the stairs, the scope, and the pattern waste separately, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat rate per yard doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/yard whether the job is a stretch-in over pad or a glue-down — even though glue-down alone swaps pad for adhesive and adds installer hours per yard. Prices scope separately from a starting kit for stretch-in, glue-down, double-stick, or carpet tile, so a glue-down is never quoted off a stretch-in rate.
Has no line for stairs, regardless of whether the job has none or fourteen. Prices stairs per step — labor hours and stair-wrap material — on top of floor yardage, so stairs are never folded into "a little more floor."
Prices the floor's billed yardage at one waste percent, with no separate line for the extra waste a patterned match leaves on the cutting-room floor. Applies a pattern-specific waste percent (solid, textured, patterned, or berber) to the floor yards, so a patterned job buys more carpet than a solid one on the same footprint.
Has no line for tear-out, a furniture move, transitions, or haul-away, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices tear-out hours and dump weight, furniture-move time, transitions per opening, and haul-away separately, so a job needing all four costs more than a bare install on an empty room.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two floors, the same area-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets:

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $55.41/yd rate, applied by billed yardage aloneGap
400 sq ft living room, stretch-in, solid, no stairs (the job this flat number was built on)$2,708.76 — $55.41/yd$2,708.76 (same job, same rate)No gap: this is the one job the flat rate fits.
400 sq ft, patterned glue-down, 14 stairs, tear-out, furniture move, haul-away$4,942.62 bid price; $3,954.09 break-even cost$3,681.45The flat rate quotes $272.64 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $1,261.17 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the $55.41/yd rate the 400 sq ft stretch-in living room's own price works out to. Applied to the patterned glue-down job's 66.44 billed yards, that rate does not just erode margin — it prices below the job's own cost to complete, even though both jobs measure the same 400 square feet of floor. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one floor it was built for, and nothing about a per-yard number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per yard get a carpet install quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is scope and stairs, not floor area. A patterned glue-down with fourteen stairs, a tear-out, a furniture move, and a haul-away needs stair labor and material, extra pattern-match waste, adhesive instead of pad, tear-out hours and dump weight, and furniture-move time that a flat living-room stretch-in never sees. A flat rate per yard charges all of that the same as the cheap special it was built on.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Stairs, pattern-match waste, tear-out, furniture moves, and haul-away. Stairs alone are not yards -- they are priced per step, with their own labor and stair-wrap material -- and a job that needs the old carpet torn out, the furniture moved, and the scraps hauled away is doing four things a bare stretch-in over pad is not. A per-yard number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 400 sq ft stretch-in living room with no stairs prices at $2,708.76, which works out to $55.41 a yard. Applying that same $55.41-a-yard rate to a 400 sq ft patterned glue-down job with 14 stairs, a tear-out, a furniture move, and a haul-away quotes $3,681.45 -- $272.64 below that job's own $3,954.09 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $1,261.17 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat rate per yard ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same scope, same pattern, no stairs, no tear-out either time -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which job it was built on and neither does the estimator until the floor and stairs are actually measured.

Does this calculator know what carpet or labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on local mill invoices or labor rates. It takes the floor square footage, stair count, scope, pattern, transitions, tear-out, furniture move, and haul-away, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Carpet Installation Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read the pricing walkthrough.

It is not flooring-spec, moisture-test, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against your own mill invoices and crew times before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

vs-jobber.html.text:
← Carpet Installation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber runs a home-service business's clients, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payments. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one carpet install cost, given its floor yards, stairs, and scope, before you quote it.

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, flooring, and cleaning trades.
